what: Double-parallelogram remote centre. Motor A moves a pair of linked parallelograms. Their passive output is a long tool beam. Watch its empty end hole: the beam changes heading around that point even though no axle or bearing passes through it. The comparison model replaces one loop link with a longer stock beam while leaving the same motor program in place. Two linked parallelograms turn a tool about a point where there is no hinge. While motor A sweeps ±35°, the tool keeps the input's heading to 0.002° and the remote centre moves less than 0.02 mm.
try: Load ghost-pivot.ldr and the matching ghost-pivot.bw program. Reset to the saved pose, then press Run in Robot Lab’s toolbar. Identify the tool beam’s empty end hole before watching the sweep.

Observe two things separately: how far the tool turns and how far that particular hole moves relative to the frame. A point that stays still is only interesting here if the tool actually changes heading.

Predict what the longer-link comparison will do before loading ghost-pivot-unequal-link.ldr. Run the same program and follow the same tool hole. Does reaching the same motor angles preserve the remote centre?
Reset before repeating after manual movement or an interruption. Keep the supplied finite sweep; the model demonstrates a bounded assembly branch, not unrestricted rotation.
why: A parallelogram carries a direction across a moving linkage. Two linked parallelograms combine that direction relationship with matching distances so that the tool’s translation and rotation cancel at one chosen point. The surrounding links carry the constraint; there is no hidden bearing at the end hole. Lengthening one link changes the loop closure and removes the exact geometric cancellation.
matters: A remote centre lets a mechanism change a tool’s heading while keeping a chosen location accessible. The useful distinction is between moving an entire tool around an actual pivot and creating the same motion through bearings placed elsewhere. This model studies that kinematic principle, not a load capacity or a medical device.
question: If the end hole remains still, is the whole tool stationary? Should the longer-link model retain the same fixed hole just because its motor reaches the same targets?
answer: No. A rigid tool can rotate while one of its points remains fixed. The remote-centre linkage makes that point the empty end hole. The longer link changes the geometry, so the same input angles need not keep the hole at one location. Compare the actual hole position and tool heading; the motor encoder alone cannot establish either output property.
further: Follow the same physical end hole through the entire sweep, including reversals. Do not choose a new centre from each pair of tool positions after the experiment.
Compare Pantograph Doubler and Scale Echo. They scale a moving point’s path; Ghost Pivot constrains a point of a rotating rigid tool to remain fixed.
A good return does not prove that the centre stayed fixed during the sweep. Check the largest observed displacement as well as the final pose.
Real pin clearance, beam flexibility and friction can move the apparent centre. Native results describe the supplied finite simulation; hardware stiffness and precision require separate measurements.

In the recorded native experiment, the main tool swept 70.264° while its end hole moved at most 0.143540 mm in 3D. The longer-link control reached 21.519175 mm from its own saved point. These are observations of the supplied finite simulation, not a hardware precision rating.
formula: Ideal main geometry, in mm: let u be the rotating input’s unit direction and e the fixed direction from O1 to O2. The parallelograms give A = 32u − 48e and B = 80u − 48e. The tool’s actual end hole is R = A − (2/3)(B − A) = −48e, independent of u. Measured centre error is |R_observed(q) − R_observed(0)| relative to the observed frame; the equation does not supply the observation.
